source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb; 8.5; 9.4; 9.5; 9.6; 20.5

main.t: The lateral bone of the forearm, on the thumb side (radius).

simpler.t: The radius is the forearm bone on the thumb side.

deeper.t: It turns around the ulna as the palm turns backwards and forwards (pronation and supination).

facts.t: It runs from the elbow to the wrist, alongside the ulna.
In the anatomical position it is lateral, on the thumb side; the ulna is medial.
Its head meets the humerus and ulna at the elbow. Its lower end meets the carpal bones at the wrist.

simpler.t: It runs from your elbow to your wrist on the thumb side.

deeper.t: When the palm faces backwards, the radius crosses over the ulna and the two form an X.

items.name: Head
items.t: A disc at the top. Its hollow meets the capitulum of the humerus; its rim turns against the ulna.

items.name: Neck
items.t: The narrow part just below the head.

items.name: Radial tuberosity
items.t: An oval bump below the neck, on the inner side, where a muscle attaches.

items.name: Interosseous border
items.t: A ridge on the inner side of the shaft. The interosseous membrane attaches along it.

items.name: Ulnar notch
items.t: A shallow hollow at the lower end that meets the head of the ulna.

items.name: Styloid process
items.t: A pointed projection at the lower outer end. Ligaments of the wrist joint attach to it.

items.name: Carpal surface
items.t: The smooth lower end. It meets the scaphoid and lunate at the wrist joint.

simpler.t: It has a round head at the elbow and a wide end at the wrist.

deeper.t: Its styloid process reaches further down than the ulna’s. This limits how far the hand bends to the thumb side.

facts.t: Its disc-shaped head turns within a ring of ligament at a pivot joint.
Its shaft is slightly curved, so as the head turns, its lower end swings across the ulna.
The broad lower end meets two carpal bones directly, so force from a fall on the hand passes into it.

simpler.t: Its round head spins. This lets your forearm twist and your palm turn over.

items.name: Elbow joint
items.t: Its head meets the capitulum (humeroradial joint), inside the same capsule as the elbow hinge.

items.name: Proximal radioulnar joint
items.t: A pivot joint: the head turns in the radial notch of the ulna.

items.name: Distal radioulnar joint
items.t: The ulnar notch meets the head of the ulna.

items.name: Wrist (radiocarpal) joint
items.t: A condyloid joint: the lower end meets the scaphoid and lunate.

items.name: Annular ligament
items.t: Encircles the head and holds it against the ulna as it turns.

items.name: Interosseous membrane
items.t: A sheet of dense connective tissue joining the shafts of the radius and ulna.

items.name: Radial artery
items.t: Runs down the forearm alongside the radius to the wrist.

simpler.t: It joins the humerus, the ulna and the wrist bones, and the radial artery runs beside it.

facts.t: It forms by replacing a cartilage model with bone (endochondral ossification).
Bone first appears in the shaft by about the twelfth week. Centres in the ends appear later, usually after birth.

items.injury: A fall onto the outstretched hand, often in an older person with osteoporosis.
items.damaged: The lower end of the radius breaks across, and the lower fragment is pushed backwards and upwards (Colles fracture).
items.cannotDo: Use the wrist normally: the forearm has a “dinner fork” bend just above it.
items.why: The hand is carried backwards with the displaced fragment.

items.injury: A young child is lifted or swung by the hand.
items.damaged: The head of the radius slips partly out of the annular ligament (“pulled elbow”).
items.cannotDo: Turn the palm up, and the child holds the arm still.
items.why: The annular ligament normally holds the head in place as it turns.
items.check: “Pulled elbow” (radial head subluxation) in young children is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

items.q: Explain how the radius and ulna move as the forearm turns from palm forwards to palm backwards.
model: The head of the radius turns at the proximal radioulnar joint, a pivot joint.
The shaft is slightly curved, so the lower end of the radius crosses over the ulna.
The two bones end in an X shape; supination returns them to parallel.

items.q: Compare the styloid processes of the radius and the ulna.
model: Radius: a pointed projection at its lower outer end.
Ulna: a short projection from the back of its head.
The radial styloid reaches further down.
So the hand bends less far to the thumb side than to the little-finger side.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman falls on her outstretched hand. Predict the fracture and how the wrist looks.
model: A Colles fracture: the lower end of the radius breaks across.
The lower fragment is pushed backwards and upwards.
The forearm has a “dinner fork” bend just above the wrist.
It is the most common forearm fracture, especially with osteoporosis.

check.stem: Which part of the radius meets the capitulum of the humerus?
check.why: The small hollow on the top of the head meets the capitulum at the elbow.

check.stem: At which joint does the head of the radius turn during pronation?
check.why: The proximal radioulnar joint is a pivot joint: the head turns in the radial notch of the ulna.

check.stem: What causes the “dinner fork” shape after a Colles fracture?
options: The lower fragment of the radius is pushed backwards
check.why: The distal fragment is driven backwards and upwards, carrying the hand with it.
